results.prompt: Compare the tiers and tell me the best value.
Show the costs and explain the largest one.
results.raw:
I don't have your actual cost figures in this conversation, so the block below uses a representative monthly cloud/infra breakdown as a stand-in — swap in your real numbers and the same shape (total, largest line, share) applies.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([row1, ch1, t1])
row1 = Row([m1, m2])
m1 = Metric("Total monthly cost", "40 000 kr", "Illustrative sample, not your data")
m2 = Metric("Largest line — GPU compute", "18 400 kr", "46% of total cost", "warning")
ch1 = Chart("donut", "Cost share by category", ["GPU compute", "Storage", "Egress", "Managed DB", "Observability", "Licenses"], [{name: "Monthly cost (kr)", values: [18400, 7200, 5600, 4100, 2300, 2400]}])
t1 = Table("Cost breakdown", ["Category", "Monthly (kr)", "Share"], [["GPU compute", "18 400", "46%"], ["Storage", "7 200", "18%"], ["Egress / bandwidth", "5 600", "14%"], ["Managed database", "4 100", "10%"], ["Observability", "2 300", "6%"], ["Licenses & support", "2 400", "6%"], ["Total", "40 000", "100%"]])
:::

**The largest cost is GPU compute at 18 400 kr — 46% of the total.**

Why it dominates:

- **It's the only line charged by the hour while running.** Storage and licences scale with capacity, but accelerators bill continuously, including idle time. A cluster that's only ~35% utilised still costs 100%.
- **It's the unit that scales fastest with usage.** Traffic doubling doesn't double egress; it can triple GPU spend because of queueing, retries and over-provisioned replicas.
- **It's the one with the least elastic discount.** Storage tiers and reserved database capacity have cheap downgrades; GPUs rarely do.

Where to attack it, in order of typical payoff:

1. **Utilisation first.** If average accelerator utilisation is under 50%, right-sizing or autoscaling to a floor of zero beats any price negotiation.
2. **Scheduling and batching.** Group requests into larger batches, cap concurrency, and move non-interactive work to off-peak/spot capacity.
3. **Caching.** Prompt/response and embedding caches convert repeat traffic into near-zero marginal cost.
4. **Then commitment.** Only after 1–3, buy reserved or committed capacity for the genuinely steady baseline.

Want me to redo this with your real figures? Paste the line items (or a CSV/invoice summary) and I'll rebuild the breakdown and identify the actual largest driver.

results.prompt: Show the timeline and summarize progress.
Chart the growth and interpret it.
results.raw:
I don't have a dataset in this conversation, so I can't chart *your* growth yet — tell me the metric (revenue, users, churn…) and the time range and I'll rebuild it exactly.

To illustrate the shape you'd be looking at, here's a representative 12-month series:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([g1, c1, note])
g1 = Grid([m1, m2, m3])
m1 = Metric("Total growth", "+200%", "1 200 → 3 600 over 12 months", "positive")
m2 = Metric("Avg monthly growth", "+10.5%", "Compound, month over month", "positive")
m3 = Metric("Latest month", "3 600", "December", "neutral")
c1 = Chart("line", "Monthly active users", ["Jan","Feb","Mar","Apr","May","Jun","Jul","Aug","Sep","Oct","Nov","Dec"], [{name:"Users", values:[1200,1340,1490,1620,1810,1990,2240,2480,2700,2980,3250,3600]}])
note = Badge("Illustrative data — swap in your real numbers", "neutral")
:::

**How to read it**

- **It's compounding, not linear.** Straight-line growth would add a constant amount each month; this curve keeps steepening because each month's gain is ~10.5% of a larger base. That works out to a **doubling roughly every 7 months**.
- **No deceleration yet.** The month-over-month rate stays steady rather than tapering, which is the healthy signal. The danger sign to watch for is the curve still rising while the *percentage* gain per month shrinks — that's growth flattening even though the line looks fine.
- **Watch the tail.** If you only had Jan–Jun you'd extrapolate ~1 200/month by December; the actual series compounds past that, so the back half carries most of the value — and most of the sensitivity to a slowdown.

**Caveats before you act on this:** with 12 points, a single strong month can flatter the trend. Check whether growth is driven by new customers or by existing ones expanding, and compare against a seasonally matched period.

Send me the actual figures (or the period and metric) and I'll re-render it with real growth rates and a fitted trend.

results.prompt: Build a custom 3D bar chart you can spin.
Make a loan calculator with sliders.
Compare AWS vs GCP vs Azure.
results.raw:
All three are mature, global platforms — the real differences are ecosystem fit, service breadth and pricing model. Here's a structured look:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([cmp1, s1, s2])
cmp1 = Comparison("Cloud platforms at a glance", [{name:"AWS",attributes:["Broadest service catalog, most mature","Launched 2006 — largest ecosystem","~30% market share","Free tier: 12 months"]},{name:"Google Cloud",attributes:["Best-in-class data & AI/ML tooling","Kubernetes (GKE) and BigQuery heritage","~13% market share","Credits: $300 / 90 days"]},{name:"Microsoft Azure",attributes:["Deep Microsoft/AD/Office integration","Strong hybrid + enterprise agreements","~20% market share","Credits: $200 / 30 days"]}])
s1 = Section("Head-to-head details", [tbl1])
tbl1 = Table("", ["Dimension", "AWS", "Google Cloud", "Azure"], [["Main strength", "Breadth & maturity", "Data, analytics, AI/ML", "Microsoft ecosystem, hybrid"],["Typical fit", "Startups to large enterprise, most workloads", "Data-heavy and ML teams, GKE shops", "Microsoft-centric enterprises, regulated/hybrid"],["Learning curve", "Steep, huge surface area", "Moderate, cleaner UI", "Moderate, inconsistent naming"],["Pricing feel", "Granular and complex", "Simple with sustained-use discounts", "Complex, EA/hybrid discounts"],["Compliance regions", "Very broad global footprint", "Growing global footprint", "Very broad, strong in EU/regulated"]])
s2 = Section("Share of cloud infrastructure market (approx.)", [ch1])
ch1 = Chart("donut", "", ["AWS", "Azure", "Google Cloud", "Others"], [{name:"Share %", values:[30, 20, 13, 37]}])
:::

Quick take: pick **AWS** when you want the widest choice of services and the biggest hiring pool; **Azure** when you're already on Microsoft identity, Windows Server or enterprise agreements, or need hybrid; **Google Cloud** when your workload is data/analytics or AI-heavy, or you want the smoothest managed Kubernetes. If none dominates, run a small proof-of-concept on the two most likely — the concrete bill and latency numbers for *your* workload usually decide it, not the feature lists.

results.prompt: Sammenlign de to abonnementene.
Which is better, React or Vue? Compare.
results.raw:
Both are excellent choices, and the "better" one depends mainly on your team and ecosystem needs.

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Comparison("React vs Vue", [{name: "React", attributes: ["UI library, not a full framework — you pick routing, state, data layers", "JSX: logic and markup in plain JavaScript", "Largest ecosystem, tooling and hiring pool", "Backed by Meta; Next.js covers full-stack needs", "More concepts to learn: hooks, memoization, effect rules"]}, {name: "Vue", attributes: ["Progressive framework with official router and state (Pinia)", "Single-file components: template, script and styles together", "Gentlest learning curve; HTML-like templates feel familiar", "Smaller but very loyal community, strong in Europe/Asia", "Independently maintained; excellent docs and sane defaults"]}])
:::

**In short:** pick **Vue** for fast onboarding, clear conventions and smaller projects where the official tooling is enough. Pick **React** when hiring, third-party libraries, React Native for mobile, or a large long-lived codebase matter most — its ecosystem is the deciding factor more than the library itself. Neither will be the reason a project fails; team familiarity usually outweighs the technical differences.

results.prompt: Create a survey form with a rating.
results.raw:
Here's a short survey that captures an overall rating plus a 0–10 recommend score, and updates the score bar as you drag:

:::intelligent-ui{v="1"}
root = Stack([form1, row2])

$overall = "Satisfied"
$nps = 8
$area = "Dashboards"
$comments = ""
$contact = true

form1 = Form("Product feedback survey", [f1, f2, f3, f4, f5])

f1 = Field("Overall satisfaction", [r1], "How happy are you with the product overall?")
r1 = Radio("Rating", $overall, ["Very satisfied", "Satisfied", "Neutral", "Dissatisfied"])

f2 = Field("How likely are you to recommend us?", [s1, p1], "0 = not at all likely · 10 = extremely likely")
s1 = Slider("Score", $nps, 0, 10)
p1 = Progress("Recommend score", $nps * 10)

f3 = Field("Where do you spend most of your time?", [sel1])
sel1 = Select("Main area", $area, ["Onboarding", "Dashboards", "Integrations", "Reports", "Billing"])

f4 = Field("What should we improve?", [t1], "Optional — one or two sentences is plenty")
t1 = Textarea("Your comments", $comments, "Tell us what to fix, keep, or add…")

f5 = Field("Follow-up", [sw1])
sw1 = Switch("Yes, you may contact me about this feedback", $contact)

row2 = Row([b1, b2])
b1 = Button("Submit survey", "notes.create", {title:"Survey response", content:"Product feedback survey response"})
b2 = Button("Clear comments", @Reset($comments))
:::

The rating question is the core signal — "Very satisfied"/"Satisfied"/"Neutral"/"Dissatisfied" maps cleanly to a 4-point satisfaction scale, while the 0–10 slider gives you a standard recommend (NPS-style) score you can trend over time. Submitting requires a confirmation, and the follow-up switch decides whether the response can be attributed to a person.

results.prompt: Explain the water cycle.
results.raw:
The water cycle (also called the hydrological cycle) is the continuous movement of water between the ocean, atmosphere, and land. The Sun supplies the energy, gravity does the rest, and the total amount of water on Earth stays roughly constant — it just keeps changing form and location.

**Evaporation and transpiration**
Solar energy heats liquid water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, giving molecules enough energy to escape as water vapour. Plants contribute a large share through transpiration, releasing water vapour from their leaves. Together these are often called *evapotranspiration*, and the ocean accounts for the vast majority of it.

**Condensation**
As vapour rises it cools. Cool air holds less moisture, so the vapour condenses onto tiny particles like dust and sea salt to form cloud droplets. This is the step that turns invisible gas back into visible water.

**Precipitation**
When droplets collide and grow heavy enough, gravity wins and they fall as rain, snow, sleet, or hail. Snow and hail can store water for months in glaciers and snowpack before it melts.

**Infiltration and runoff**
Water that reaches the ground either soaks into the soil (infiltration) and recharges aquifers, or flows across the surface as runoff into streams and rivers. Together with groundwater flow, this returns water downhill toward the ocean.

**Storage**
Water doesn't travel in a single loop at a steady pace — it pauses in reservoirs. A drop can sit in an ocean for thousands of years, in an ice sheet for tens of thousands, or in the atmosphere for only about nine days. These delays are why the cycle is best pictured as many overlapping paths rather than one clean circle.

Two things worth noting: only about 0.001% of Earth's water is in the atmosphere at any moment, yet that tiny fraction drives all weather. And because the cycle is a closed system in terms of total mass, the water you drink today has been cycling for billions of years — some of it likely passed through dinosaurs.
